docs.description: Case name: Holder v. Hall Opinion filed: 1994-06-30 Docket No.: 91-2012 Citations: • 129 L. Ed. 2d 687 • 114 S. Ct. 2581 • 512 U.S. 874 • 1994 U.S. LEXIS 5083 Case holding summaries: • "under Section 5 ... the proposed voting practice should be measured against the existing voting practice to determine whether retrogression would result from the proposed change...." The "baseline for comparison is present by definition; it is the existing status" • “The baseline for comparison is present by definition; it is the existing status.” • noting the solicitor general had reasoned (improperly), "the Hispanic legislators elected from Hispanic districts in Dade County would represent, not just the interests of the Dade County Hispanics, but the interests of all the Hispanics in the State" (citation omitted) • “But ‘we have never applied stare decisis mechanically to prohibit overruling our earlier decisions determining the meaning of statutes.’” • noting the solicitor general had reasoned (improperly), "the Hispanic legislators elected from Hispanic districts in Dade County would represent, not just the interests of the Dade County Hispanics, but the interests of all the Hispanics in the State" (citation omitted) • “This case presents the question whether the size of a governing authority is subject to a vote dilution challenge under § 2 of the Voting Rights Act” • separate opinion of Stevens, J. • legislative history "is read selectively to support the result the Court intends to achieve" • holding that the size of a governing body is not subject to a Section 2 vote dilution challenge • "But `we have never applied stare decisis mechanically to prohibit overruling our earlier decisions determining the meaning of statutes.'" • separate opinion of Stevens, J. • "The baseline for comparison is present by definition; it is the existing status." • “Resort to legislative history is only justified where the face of the [statute] is inescap- ably ambiguous.” • binding opinion of Kennedy, J. • noting that "the power to influence the political process is not limited to winning elections" • rejecting the "failure of [the minority group] to have legislative seats in proportion to its population" as a sufficient basis for a claim • change from three-member commission to five-member commission is subject to § 5 preclearance • rejecting a "single-member-office" exception to § 2 • "Again in 1975, both the House and Senate Judiciary Committees, in recommending extension of the Act, noted with approval the `broad interpretations to the scope of Section 5' in Allen and Perkins v. Matthews [400 U. S. 379 (1971)]" • the Act must "be interpreted in light of its prophylactic purpose and the historical experience which it reflects" • it "is not disputed" that an expansion in the size of a board of education is subject to § 5 preclearance • noting that there is no decision of this Court holding a legislative apportionment plan violative of the Fifteenth Amendment • in the 1982 extension of the Act, "Congress specifically endorsed a broad construction" of § 5 • "After extensive deliberations in 1970 on bills to extend the Voting Rights Act, during which the Allen case was repeatedly discussed, the Act was extended for five years, without any substantive modification of § 5" • remand of challenge to solecommissioner system with instructions to consider size and geographic compactness within proposed three- and five-member commission forms of government • change in size is a change in a "standard, practice, or procedure" because the change "increase[s] or diminish[es] the number of officials for whom the electorate may vote" • concluding that it would be "anomalous" to do otherwise • "Even if serious problems lie ahead in applying the `totality of the circumstances' [inquiry under § 2(b) of the Voting Rights Act], that task, difficult as it may prove to be, cannot justify a judicially created limitation on the coverage of the broadly worded statute[.]" • declaring that the "single-member district is generally the appropriate standard against which to measure minority group potential to elect" • "Under the ejusdem generis rule of construction the general words are confined to the class and may not be used to enlarge it" • recognizing that systems that "classify and separate voters by race" threaten "to undermine our system of representative democracy by signaling to elected officials that they represent a particular racial group rather than their constituency as a whole" • O'Connor, J., joined by Burger, C. J., and Powell and Rehnquist, JJ., concurring in judgment • "There is no principled reason why one size [of an elected governing body] should be picked over another as the benchmark for [determining whether vote dilution exists]." • separate opinion of Stevens, J.

cause of ultimate adverse action, then employer is liable • relying on supervisors’ statements as evidence that they took adverse employment actions based on antimilitary discriminatory animus • “[I]f the employer’s investigation results in an adverse action for reasons unrelated to the supervisor’s original biased action . . . , then the employer will not be liable.” • applying cat’s-paw theory in the context of a discrimination claim brought under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act, 38 U.S.C. § 4301 et seq. • involving a claim of military discrimination under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act • “The employer is at fault because one of its agents committed an action based on discriminatory animus that was intended to cause, and did law • applying the cat’s paw theory to a Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act claim • describing the term “cat’s paw” to describe a case in which a particular management official, acting because of improper animus, influences an agency official who is unaware of the improper animus when implementing a personnel action • applying a cat’s paw approach to cases brought under the and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994, which is “very similar to Title VII” • “[I]f the employer’s investigation results in an adverse action for reasons unrelated to the supervisor’s original biased action . . . , then the employer will not be liable.” • explaining elements of a “cat’s paw” theory of discrimination • “Intentional torts such as this, as distinguished from negligent or reckless torts, generally require that the actor intend the consequences of an act, not simply the act itself.” • “[T]he requirement that the biased supervisor’s action be a causal factor of the ultimate employment action incorporates the traditional tort-law concept of proximate cause.” • noting that veteran's supervisors "were hostile to Staub's military obligations" and listing the supervisors' actions and derogatory comments that showed hostility • “[I]f the independent investigation relies on facts provided by the biased supervisor—as is necessary in any case of cat’s-paw liability—then • finding that lower-level employees intended to cause a contractual injury where they had said they were “out to get” and “get rid” of the plaintiff • holding that “if a supervisor performs an act motivated by antimilitary animus that is intended by the supervisor to cause an adverse employment action, and if that act is a proximate cause of the ultimate employment action, then the employer is liable under USERRA” (emphasis omitted) • observing that proximate cause requires only some direct relation between injury asserted and injurious conduct alleged and excludes only those links that are too remote, purely contingent, or indirect • a cause is superseding only if it is of independent origin and was not foreseeable • declining to express any view as to whether an “employer would be liable for employment discrimination based on the discriminatory animus of an employee who influenced, but did not make, the ultimate employment decision" • concluding that a “biased report” can count as that “act” • "An employer's authority to reward, punish, or dismiss is often allocated among multiple agents," not just "[t]he one who makes the ultimate decision" • concluding that anti-military docs.description: Case name: Tuilaepa v. California Opinion filed: 1994-06-30 Docket No.: 93-5131 Citations: • 129 L. Ed. 2d 750 • 114 S. Ct. 2630 • 512 U.S. 967 • 1994 U.S. LEXIS 5084 Case holding summaries: • holding that California death penalty special circumstances were not unconstitutionally vague • “A capital sentencer need not be instructed how to weigh any particular fact in the capi- tal sentencing decision.” • uphold- ing a California aggravating factor that permitted the jury to consider "[t]he presence or absence of criminal activity by the defendant which involved the use or attempted use of force or violence or the express or implied threat to use force or vio- lence" (alteration in original) • “To render a defendant eligible for the death penalty in a homicide case, we have indicated that the trier of fact must convict the defendant of murder and find one ‘aggravating circumstance’ (or its equivalent • observing that decision whether death-eligible defendant should receive death penalty "is an individualized determination on the basis of the character of the indi- UNITED STATES v. FULKS 39 vidual and the circumstances of the crime" (internal quotation marks omitted) • holding that "[t]he circumstances of the crime are a traditional subject for consideration by the sentencer," and may include factors such as the defendant's age • "there is no suggestion that the term 'age' is vague" • "[A]ggravating circumstance[s] may be contained in the definition of the crime or in a separate sentencing factor (or in both)." • upholding use of prior criminal activity sentencing factor • noting that sentencing factors that permit the jury to "consider matters of historical fact" are not constitutionally infirm • "A capital sentencer need not be instructed how to weigh any particular fact in the capital sentencing decision." • explaining aggravating circumstance "may not apply to every defendant convicted of a murder; it must apply only to a subclass of [such] defendants" • explaining that "[a] capital sentencer need not be instructed how to weigh any particular fact in the capital sentencing decision" • "A capital sentencer need not be instructed how to weigh any particular fact in the capital sentencing decision." • noting "a separate requirement for the selection decision, where the sentencer determines whether a defendant eligible for the death penalty should in fact receive that sentence" • circumstances of a particular offense [are] constitutionally indispensable parts of the process of inflicting the penalty of death • observing that decision whether death-eligible defendant should receive death penalty "is an individualized determination on the basis of the character of the individual and the circumstances of the crime" (internal quotation marks omitted) • noting that conducting eligibility and selection phases jointly can result in “some tension” • explaining that an aggravating circumstance "must apply only to a subclass of defendants convicted of murder." • "[O]ur capital jurisprudence has established that the sentencer should consider the circumstances of the crime in deciding whether to impose the death penalty." • upholding use of prior criminal activity sentencing factor • "the basic principle [is] that a factor is not unconstitutional if it has some `common-sense core of meaning ... that criminal juries should be capable of understanding'" • distinguishing eligibility process from selection process • noting that at the selection phase, the state is not confined to submitting specific propositional questions to the jury and may indeed allow the jury unbridled discretion • describing "eligibility decision" and "selection decision" and noting they together constitute the two phases in death penalty deliberations • vulnerability through age of victim • "The aggravating circumstance may be contained in the definition of the crime or in a separate sentencing factor (or in both)." • noting the requirement that the jury consider mitigating evidence before imposing a death sentence • joint opinion of Stewart, Powell, and Stevens, JJ. • "requirement of individualized sentencing in capital cases is satisfied by allowing the jury to consider all relevant mitigating evidence" • joint opinion of Stewart, Powell, and Stevens, JJ. • trial court concluded that 10 of 11 factors were aggravating, including factors (d)(h) and (j) • invalidating aggravating circumstance that the "`murder . . . was committed by a person . . . who has a substantial history of serious assaultive convictions' " • "If the sentencer fairly could conclude that an aggravating circumstance applies to every defendant eligible for the death penalty, the circumstance is constitutionally infirm" • vagueness analysis applied to aggravating factor, even though remaining aggravating factor made defendant death eligible • court "`must first determine whether the statutory language defining the circumstance is itself too vague to provide any guidance to the sentencer' " • "We are not faced with pejorative adjectives . . . that describe a crime as a whole" • difference between "nonweighing" States like Georgia and "weighing" States like California is "not one of `semantics' " • jury found that "the defendant [fell] within the legislatively defined category of persons eligible for the death penalty [by] determining the truth of the alleged special circumstance," commission of murder during the course of a robbery • question whether murder was "outrageously or wantonly vile, horrible and inhuman" • "jury's interpretation of [outrageously or wantonly vile, horrible and inhuman factor] can only be the subject of sheer speculation" • factors "are by necessity somewhat general" • the Court "plainly rejected the submission that a particular set of facts surrounding a murder, however shocking they might be, were enough in themselves, and without some narrowing principle to apply to those facts, to warrant the imposition of the death penalty" • age may be relevant factor in sentencing decision • holding that challenge to portion of California's death penalty regime requiring jury to consider circumstances of the crime was merit less because it was at odds with settled principles of capital jurisprudence that circumstances of the crime must be considered • joint opinion of Stewart, Powell, and Stevens, JJ. • “The objectives of these two inquiries can be in some tension, at least when the inquiries occur at the same time” • "Both a backward-looking and a forward-looking inquiry are a permissible part of the sentencing process, however, and the States have considerable latitude in determining how to guide the sentencer's decision in this respect." • vulnerability through age of victim • holding that the State’s future dangerousness element is not unconstitutionally vague
